title: Real space and represented space: Cross-cultural perspectives

findings.antecedent: question about distance from self to represented figures (Opolot's study)
findings.mechanism: question about distance from self brought observers into represented space
findings.quote: When they were asked about the distance from themselves their responses were more affected by the represented space than under the standard procedure, that is, in terms of Hudson's test (see sect. 7, para. 2) they made "3D" responses more often.

findings.antecedent: African subjects (Shapiro 1960, Deregowski 1974a, 1977, Jahoda 1976, 1978)
findings.consequent: orientational errors in copying Kohs's patterns (Figure 11)
findings.mechanism: systematic tendency to construct figures that are seen as more symmetrical and perceptually stable than the stimulus figures
findings.quote: Many of the drawings showed the patterns, but in incorrect orientations. Some of these errors were as large as those of brain-damaged patients in Shapiro's London hospital.

findings.antecedent: American child (19 months) raised without explicit instruction on pictures
findings.consequent: ability to name representations of familiar objects
findings.mechanism: pictures are instantly and fully perceptible (author argues against this interpretation)
findings.quote: He was nevertheless able to name representations of familiar objects correctly (Hochberg & Brooks 1962).

findings.antecedent: Young French children viewing 'syncretic animals' (Figure 15)
findings.consequent: naming of individual elements vs composite figure
findings.mechanism: children tended to list individual elements rather than naming the composite figure
findings.quote: When such figures were used in the United States, children tended to list individual elements rather than naming the com-posite figure.

findings.antecedent: Adult Baruya (Papua New Guinea) subjects
findings.consequent: scores on Matching Familiar Figures Test (Kagan 1966)
findings.mechanism: difficulty to attend to several details of stimuli and tended to use only one detail for matching
findings.quote: Ausburn and Ausburn's (1983) observations that were gathered among the Baruya (Papua New Guinea) suggest that such responses might have ac-counted for the low scores attained by adult subjects on the Matching Familiar Figures Test developed by Kagan (1966).

findings.antecedent: Rural Kenyan observers viewing tortoise representation (Figure 16)
findings.mechanism: descriptions derived from various elements of the figure taken in isolation
findings.quote: His tortoise representation (Figure 16) was described by some as a snake, by some as an elephant, and by some as a crocodile.

findings.antecedent: Zambian schoolchildren classified as 2D perceivers (built flat models from pictures)
findings.mechanism: 2D-model builders did not perceive the spatial properties of the impossible figure; they merely copied a flat pattern
findings.quote: Those who perceived the pictures as 2/3d, and constructed 3D models, took relatively longer to copy the "two-pronged trident" figure than those who built flat models.

findings.antecedent: English schoolboys viewing impossible figures
findings.consequent: integration of elements as having spatial properties
findings.mechanism: did not integrate those elements as closely to-gether as more sophisticated observers do
findings.quote: Young demonstrated that English schoolboys do perceive various elements of such impossible figures as having spatial properties; they do not, however, integrate those elements as closely to-gether as more sophisticated observers do.

findings.antecedent: American and Zimbabwean children sorting real wooden blocks
findings.quote: The two groups of children did not differ, it was found, when sorting the solids, but they did differ when sorting the pictures, although they did see them as pictures of blocks.

findings.antecedent: American and Zimbabwean children sorting pictures of blocks
findings.mechanism: cultural differences in the way pictures are treated
findings.quote: The two groups of children did not differ, it was found, when sorting the solids, but they did differ when sorting the pictures, although they did see them as pictures of blocks.

findings.antecedent: Urban Zambian women of relatively little sophistication matching picture-picture and object-object
findings.quote: On a simple matching task, urban Zambian women of relatively little sophistication found picture-picture and object-object matching easier than matching pictures with objects (Deregowski 1971a).

findings.antecedent: Urban Zambian women of relatively little sophistication matching picture-object
findings.quote: On a simple matching task, urban Zambian women of relatively little sophistication found picture-picture and object-object matching easier than matching pictures with objects (Deregowski 1971a).

findings.antecedent: Scotswomen learning positions with familiar real objects
findings.quote: Scotswomen performed better when the stimuli were familiar and real objects (such as a knife or a reel of cotton) than when they were easily recognisable pictures of those objects.

findings.antecedent: Scotswomen learning positions with easily recognisable pictures of objects
findings.quote: Scotswomen performed better when the stimuli were familiar and real objects (such as a knife or a reel of cotton) than when they were easily recognisable pictures of those objects.

findings.antecedent: Scotswomen learning positions with names of objects written on cards
findings.quote: When names of the objects written on cards were used as stimuli, performance was even worse (Deregowski & Jahoda 1975).

findings.antecedent: Children from a deprived background provided with pictures for Piagetian sorting task
findings.quote: children from a deprived background are less proficient at a Piagetian sorting task when provided with pictures than when provided with objects.

findings.antecedent: Zambian children sorting objects
findings.quote: Zambian children performed about as well as Scottish children did when sorting objects, but significantly less well when sorting photographs of those objects.

findings.antecedent: Zambian children sorting photographs of objects
findings.quote: Zambian children performed about as well as Scottish children did when sorting objects, but significantly less well when sorting photographs of those objects.

findings.antecedent: Indian children living in South Africa
findings.mechanism: analogous differences to Deregowski and Serpell (1971)
findings.quote: Analogous differences in the responses of Indian children living in South Africa were reported by Ramkissoon and Bhana (1982).

findings.antecedent: Bantu subjects (Hudson's test, Figure 18)
findings.consequent: perception of pictures as flat (2D pictorial perceiver)
findings.mechanism: biosocial adaptation of the Bantu has led to relatively less differ-entiated visual perception
findings.quote: His Bantu subjects tended to see the pictures as flat significantly more often than his subjects of European descent, whereas subjects of Asian origin formed an intermediate group.

findings.antecedent: Lamba and Bisa men and boys (N=33) in Zambian village
findings.quote: Among men and boys 73% (N = 33) and 86% (N = 43), respec-tively; among girls 82% (N = 11) and 73% (N = 11), respectively.

findings.antecedent: Lamba and Bisa boys (N=43) in Zambian village
findings.quote: Among men and boys 73% (N = 33) and 86% (N = 43), respec-tively; among girls 82% (N = 11) and 73% (N = 11), respectively.

findings.antecedent: Lamba and Bisa girls (N=11) in Zambian village
findings.quote: Among men and boys 73% (N = 33) and 86% (N = 43), respec-tively; among girls 82% (N = 11) and 73% (N = 11), respectively.

findings.antecedent: Lamba and Bisa girls (N=11) in Zambian village
findings.quote: Among men and boys 73% (N = 33) and 86% (N = 43), respec-tively; among girls 82% (N = 11) and 73% (N = 11), respectively.

findings.antecedent: Subjects viewing Figure 19b (2/3d) vs Figure 19a (flat)
findings.mechanism: Figure 19b is seen as a 3D object, Figure 19a as flat
findings.quote: A subject who sees the bottom figure as depicting a 3D object is likely to see the angle between the represented arms as larger than that of the top figure.

findings.antecedent: Children of Kxoe Bushmen
findings.consequent: proneness to 2/3d perception on Kwengo Callipers Test
findings.quote: Kxoe being more prone to 2/3d perception than the !Xu.

findings.antecedent: Western 6-year-olds perceiving illusory effect from density gradients
findings.mechanism: only a quarter of them perceive it as depicting depth
findings.quote: although Western 6-year-olds per-ceive the illusory effect induced by density gradients, their verbal descriptions of the scene show that only a quarter of them perceive it as depicting depth.

findings.antecedent: Western 10-year-olds perceiving illusory effect from density gradients
findings.mechanism: All Western 10-year-olds, on the other hand, perceive both the illusion and the depth.
findings.quote: All Western 10-year-olds, on the other hand, perceive both the illusion and the depth.

findings.antecedent: Scottish children on Hudson's test (Figure 18) and Jahoda and McGurk's task (Figure 20)
findings.quote: There was a significant difference between the two groups, the Scottish responses being consistently more 3D on both tests, although this difference was greater on Hudson's test.

findings.antecedent: Scores on Jahoda and McGurk's task (Figure 20)
findings.mechanism: Hudson's test is inherently more difficult
findings.quote: In addition, the scores of both samples were higher on Jahoda and McGurk's task than they were on Hudson's test.

findings.antecedent: Ghanaian pupils (2nd and 4th grades of primary school) on Jahoda and McGurk's task
findings.quote: Ghanaian pupils from second and fourth grades of primary school do not differ in their scores but those from fourth and sixth grades do

findings.antecedent: Ghanaian pupils (4th and 6th grades of primary school) on Jahoda and McGurk's task
findings.quote: Ghanaian pupils from second and fourth grades of primary school do not differ in their scores but those from fourth and sixth grades do

findings.antecedent: Europeans vs Africans viewing Figure 18a (Hudson's test) using Pandora's Box
findings.quote: neither relatively sophisticated Europeans, who would have been expected to give 3D responses to both of Hudson's figures, nor Africans drawn from a population likely to yield 2D responders perceived Figure 18a as 2/3d.

findings.antecedent: Europeans vs Africans viewing Figure 18b (Hudson's test) using Pandora's Box
findings.consequent: perceived distance of elephant relative to other figures
findings.quote: The Europeans, unlike the Africans, saw the elephant as significantly further away from the other two figures in the picture.

findings.antecedent: Nigerian schoolchildren of academics viewing Figure 21b (implicit shape constancy)
findings.quote: Children of academics were more influenced by the presence of the background cues than were children of nonacademics

findings.antecedent: Nigerian schoolchildren of academics matching Figure 21a
findings.quote: the former, for example, chose a less squarish figure to match Figure 21a than to match Figure 21b.

findings.antecedent: Subjects from less carpentered cultures viewing Müller-Lyer illusion (Figure 22)
findings.mechanism: less prone to this effect than those from more carpentered cultures, whose constancy scaling is more responsive to the minimal angular cues
findings.quote: Observers from the less carpentered cultures are hence likely to be less prone to this effect than those from more carpentered cultures, whose constancy scaling is more responsive to the minimal angular cues the figures provide.

findings.antecedent: Inhabitants of open terrain viewing horizontal-vertical illusion (Figure 23)
findings.mechanism: see the upright arm of the figure as extending away, and hence as longer
findings.quote: The former will therefore be more susceptible to the horizontal-vertical illusion (Figure 23), because they will see the upright arm of the figure as extending away, and hence as longer.

findings.antecedent: Banyakole subjects vs United States subjects on Müller-Lyer illusion (one set of stimuli)
findings.mechanism: not clear whether the observed effect is due to differences in the strength of the stimuli or the variation in the correlation between these figures and 'carpenteredness.'
findings.quote: The failure to find expected cross-cultural differences with one of the sets of stimuli again sounds a confused yet cautionary note

findings.antecedent: Subjects from carpentered vs uncarpentered environments in Zambia viewing Müller-Lyer figures
findings.mechanism: environmental effect was therefore confirmed
findings.quote: The results showed the expected difference between subjects drawn from carpentered and uncarpentered environments, and the environmental effect was therefore confirmed.

findings.antecedent: Subjects viewing Müller-Lyer figures (circle version vs traditional arrowhead version)
findings.mechanism: equally plausible that the two types of stimuli may involve unrelated perceptual processes
findings.quote: However, there was also a greater illusory effect in both populations with the circle version than with the traditional arrowhead version.

findings.antecedent: Malawi Sena men (uneducated) identifying ellipse that 'looked most like' an inclined disc (Figure 24)
findings.mechanism: uneducated being notably less affected by the slope of the circular pattern
findings.quote: the uneducated being notably less affected by the slope of the circular pattern, just as the less sophisticated of Makanju's subjects were relatively less responsive to implicit shape constancy.

findings.antecedent: Zambian subsamples (differing in exposure to carpentered environment and tribal origin) viewing Ames room
findings.consequent: scores on judging sizes of pairs of rods
findings.mechanism: trend consistent with the carpentered world hypothesis but too weak to be statistically significant
findings.quote: The scores of various sub-samples of the Zambian sample... showed a trend consistent with the carpentered world hypothesis but too weak to be statistically significant.

findings.antecedent: American vs Zambian samples on constancy task
findings.quote: No differences were observed by Stewart between the American and the Zambian samples on the constancy task.

findings.antecedent: Ethnocultural provenance (Bushmen, Europeans, Bantu staff, Bantu locomotive drivers, European optometry students) on constancy task
findings.mechanism: finely graded differences in constancy among groups
findings.quote: Winter (1967) of finely graded differences in constancy among groups of different ethnocultural provenance, with Bushmen being clearly the best, and superior, in order of the magnitude of discrepancy, to both the European and the Bantu staff of a research institute, to Bantu locomotive drivers, and to European students of optometry

findings.antecedent: Nature of the terrain (Bushmen given constancy task)
findings.mechanism: constancy being influenced by the structuring afforded by the amount of space separating the observer from the stimulus
findings.quote: Winter's results also show that the nature of the terrain in which Bushmen were given the constancy task affected the responses, the constancy being influenced by the structuring afforded by the amount of space separating the observer from the stimulus.

findings.antecedent: Black laborers vs white research workers
findings.quote: Mundy-Castle and Nelson (1962), who compared black laborers with white research workers and found that the former showed significant underconstancy

findings.antecedent: Biaka Pygmies vs Bagandu farmers on constancy task
findings.quote: Biaka Pygmies of the Central African Republic (who are hunter-gatherers) misjudged the standard by a significantly larger increment than did their neighbors, the Bagandu farmers.

findings.antecedent: Biaka Pygmies vs Bagandu farmers on constancy task
findings.quote: Both the Pygmies and the Bagandu overestimated the size of the standard (and more distant) disc, but the Pygmies were more prone to do so.

findings.antecedent: Biaka subjects performing well on constancy task
findings.mechanism: 5 (all Biaka) were significant and such as to suggest that those who perform well on the constancy task are also more field-independent.
findings.quote: Of the 20 correlations thus obtained (10 for the Biaka and 10 for the Bagandu sample), only 5 (all Biaka) were significant and such as to suggest that those who perform well on the constancy task are also more field-independent.

findings.antecedent: Subjects prone to Ponzo illusion in pictures
findings.consequent: proneness to Ponzo illusion in three-dimensional objects
findings.mechanism: the same cues are processed, and in a similar man-ner, whether they derive from a solid or from a picture.
findings.quote: It shows that subjects prone to that illusion in viewing pictures are also prone to it in viewing three-dimensional objects.

findings.antecedent: Baoule subjects' performance on spatial tasks (construction of scenes from pictures)
findings.consequent: comprehension of representational space in drawings of village life
findings.quote: Their studies of the Baoule show significant correlations be-tween performance on spatial tasks – namely, construc-tion by means of tokens of scenes shown in pictures (such as a football game that had to be reproduced by placing small figures of players on a model football field) – and comprehension of representational space in drawings of village life.

findings.antecedent: South African black children viewing pictures with brightness absent
findings.consequent: sensitivity to changes in height at which figures were placed
findings.mechanism: different cultures may attach different importance to different cues
findings.quote: The former were more sensitive to the changes in the height at which figures were placed in pictures when the effect of brightness was absent

findings.antecedent: South African white children viewing pictures with brightness augmented
findings.consequent: sensitivity to changes in height at which figures were placed
findings.mechanism: different cultures may attach different importance to different cues
findings.quote: the latter were more sensitive to that cue when it was augmented by changes in brightness.

findings.antecedent: Scottish children building models from Figure 17 rotated 45 degrees
findings.quote: when the figure was rotated through 45 degrees so that it became symmetrical about a vertical axis, most of them built a 2D model.

findings.antecedent: Zambian children building models from Figure 17 rotated 45 degrees
findings.quote: No such change of 3D to 2D interpretation with change in orientation was observed in Zambian children.

findings.antecedent: Students from various cultures
findings.mechanism: considerable differences in pictorial skills among students drawn from various cultures
findings.quote: all show considerable differences in pictorial skills among students drawn from various cultures and suggest that students from some cultures may find it particularly difficult to understand diagrams.

findings.antecedent: Industrial workers of limited formal education building representations of cubes
findings.quote: The findings showed a considerable range of difficulties, extending from failure to recognize the number of cubes represented to difficulties concerning their mutual spatial relationships.

findings.antecedent: Physiological factors (optical and neural mechanisms)
findings.consequent: magnitude of illusions (converging and intersecting line elements)
findings.mechanism: optical blurring, light scatter in the eye, and contrast present in the retinal image
findings.quote: physiological factors associated with optical and neural mechanisms in vision may account for approximately 40% of the magnitude of illusions involving converging and intersecting line elements

findings.antecedent: Heavily pigmented ocular fundus
findings.quote: Pollack and Silvar (1967a; 1967b) were able to show that individuals with a heavily pigmented ocular fundus show reduced illusion magnitude

findings.antecedent: Skin pigmentation
findings.mechanism: more highly correlated with skin pigmentation than with ecological and experiential factors
findings.quote: Bornstein (1973) have reanalyzed existing sets of cross-cultural data and concluded that the susceptibility to some visual illusions is more highly correlated with skin pigmentation than with ecological and experiential factors.

findings.antecedent: Lightly pigmented irises
findings.mechanism: allow more light to scatter in the eye
findings.quote: Coren and Porac (1978) were able to show that lightly pigmented irises... allow more light to scatter in the eye and hence increase the magnitude of converging line illusions.

findings.antecedent: Genetic factors
findings.quote: Coren and Porac (1979) have been able to demon-strate that susceptibility to some visual-geometric illusions is heritable.

findings.antecedent: Infants as young as two months
findings.consequent: preference for pictures of faces over other objects or patterns
findings.quote: infants as young as two months prefer pictures of faces over pictures of other objects or patterns (Maurer & Salapatek 1976).

findings.antecedent: Young children from Malawi vs North America (flatness cues concealed)
findings.consequent: accuracy of judgments of pictorially depicted size and spatial relationships
findings.quote: performance in this respect is highly similar among children from cultures as contrastive as those of Malawi and North America (Ireson & McGurk 1985).

findings.antecedent: Non-Western subjects
findings.quote: Minor cross-cultural differences are reported for perceptual constancies, not infrequently pointing to superior performance by non-Western subjects (e.g., Reuning & Wortley 1973).

findings.antecedent: Cultural groups
findings.mechanism: do not favour any cultural group systemat-ically
findings.quote: The intergroup differences on visual illusions, which are commonly found, do not favour any cultural group systemat-ically (e.g., Segall et al. 1966).

findings.antecedent: Western infants (5-month-old) on pictorial depth cues
findings.quote: 5-month-old Western infants are not responsive to the whole range of pictorial depth cues but that 7-month-old infants are.

findings.antecedent: Western infants (7-month-old) on pictorial depth cues
findings.mechanism: suggests an inbuilt mechanism
findings.quote: 5-month-old Western infants are not responsive to the whole range of pictorial depth cues but that 7-month-old infants are.

findings.antecedent: Isoluminant conditions
findings.mechanism: magnocellular cortical pathway is therefore responsible for such perceived depth and for depth-related illusions
findings.quote: Livingstone and Hubel (1987) have claimed that depth processing of pictorial cues disappears under isoluminant conditions.

findings.antecedent: Light-eyed subjects on Müller-Lyer illusion
findings.quote: In the case of Müller-Lyer illusions, their light-eyed subjects experienced an illusion of about 7.5% and their dark-eyed subjects an illusion of about 6.4%.

findings.antecedent: Dark-eyed subjects on Müller-Lyer illusion
findings.quote: In the case of Müller-Lyer illusions, their light-eyed subjects experienced an illusion of about 7.5% and their dark-eyed subjects an illusion of about 6.4%.

findings.antecedent: Malawian vs Scottish subjects on blue or red versions of Müller-Lyer's figure
findings.quote: no significant difference was found between Malawian and Scottish subjects in their responses to either blue or red versions of Müller-Lyer's figure.

findings.antecedent: Ghanaian vs Scottish subjects on matching shapes presented in red or blue
findings.quote: There was no difference between the two groups with blue and red stimuli, contrary to the hypothesis that Ghanaians should find the blue stimuli relatively more difficult.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with represented object
findings.quote: familiarity with the represented object facilitates matching between the picture and the model and that the handicap of unfamiliarity is more severe in the case of adults than in the case of children

findings.antecedent: Scottish vs Zambian schoolchildren on sorting task using models
findings.source: Deregowski Response, Perception of solid models, para 2
findings.quote: absence of a significant difference between Scottish and Zambian schoolchildren on a sorting task when models were used

findings.antecedent: Scottish vs Zambian schoolchildren on sorting task using pictures
findings.source: Deregowski Response, Perception of solid models, para 2
findings.quote: presence of such a difference when pictures were used (De-regowski & Serpell 1971).

findings.antecedent: Rural Kxoe vs Zulu and white English-speaking South Africans on identifying representations of common objects drawn with segmented lines
findings.mechanism: nonpictorial activities of the Kxoe foster skills relevant to picture perception
findings.source: Deregowski Response, Perception of solid models, para 5
findings.quote: On this task the rural Kxoe were superi-or to both the Zulu and the white group even though these urban groups encounter pictures much more often.

findings.antecedent: Bukusu schoolboys drawing a model cube from memory
findings.consequent: resemblance to drawings from memory of an isometric cube drawing
findings.mechanism: reflects similar difficulties in projecting a 3D object onto a plane
findings.quote: drawings of a model cube, whether done with the model present or from memory, resemble drawings from memory of an isometric cube drawing.

findings.antecedent: Bukusu schoolboys drawing a model cube with isometric drawing on display
findings.mechanism: it is not the general drawing skill that is lacking but rather the more specific skill of projecting a 3D object onto a plane
findings.quote: When drawings are made with the isometric drawing on display, however, these difficulties disappear.

findings.antecedent: Infants viewing a strong 2/3d pictorial depth cue
findings.consequent: reaching for objects drawn to appear closer
findings.mechanism: a single 2/3d pictorial depth cue presented in a very strong form appears to be efficacious
findings.quote: They try to reach more often for objects drawn to appear closer than for those that appear further away. A single 2/3d pictorial depth cue presented in a very strong form appears to be efficacious.

findings.antecedent: Subjects whose questionnaires about maps forced them to use information depicted by contours
findings.mechanism: experience, whether it results from the kind of inspection required or from the use of maps, is important
findings.quote: Kinnear and Wood (1987) showed that subjects whose questionnaires about maps forced them to make some use of information depicted by contours remembered the maps better than those whose questionnaires asked for information about the map's references to locations or distances between points rather than using contour information.

findings.antecedent: Experts vs novices on planimetric maps
findings.quote: Gilhooly et al. confirmed Thorndyke and Stasz's findings for a planimetric map but not for a contour map, with which skilled map readers clearly had an advantage.

findings.antecedent: Skilled map readers on contour maps
findings.quote: Gilhooly et al. confirmed Thorndyke and Stasz's findings for a planimetric map but not for a contour map, with which skilled map readers clearly had an advantage.

limitations: Available data do not allow evaluation of relative magnitude of genetic and environmental contributions to perceptual skills, nor unbiased assessment of education or maturation effects.
The terms 'culture' and 'cultural' are not used in a purist sense, lacking experimental control of environmental and genetic effects.
Imperfections in cross-cultural data are repeatedly acknowledged.
The phenomenon of failure to perceive pictures has not been investigated thoroughly.
Evidence fails to show how much primates rely on specific 2/3i features or fully grasp representation.
Absence of thorough analytical studies makes it impossible to determine if improvements are due to cumulative cue effects, presence of previously absent cues, or cue interactions.
Uncertainty about the extent to which cue selection depends on genetic predispositions vs acquisition through learning.
Effects of training are measured on the same kind of stimuli as used in training, limiting generalizability to overall pictorial perception.
Lack of appropriate findings is a persistent theme.
Rapid social and demographic changes have eliminated certain populations, making it unlikely to find populations entirely free of pictorial contact today.
